opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back at that early work, I see it as sitting right at the boundary between what people called "internet AI" and what we now call embodied AI.

Internet AI, the paradigm that dominated the last decade, learns from massive amounts of passively collected data: images, text, videos scraped from the web. The tasks are mostly perception and understanding: classify this image, caption this video, answer this question. The model observes the world but never acts in it.

Learning human–object interactions from videos started from that same internet AI mindset. We had lots of videos of people grasping cups, opening drawers, using tools, and we asked whether we could recover the 3D hand poses, object poses, and contact patterns from them. In terms of data and methods, it was very much internet AI.

But the motivation was different. We weren't just trying to recognize "a person is opening a drawer." We wanted to understand *how* the interaction happens physically: where the fingers go, how forces are applied, how the object moves in response. That kind of knowledge isn't useful for a classification benchmark. It's useful for an agent that has to do the task itself, like a robot hand.

Over time I realized videos alone have a ceiling. They give you appearance and some geometry, but not the physics: the forces, the friction, the closed-loop feedback when something slips. A model can watch a million videos of people grasping and still not know how to grasp, because it has never felt the consequences of its actions. That gap is the core difference between internet AI and embodied AI.

So that work was a bridge for me. It taught me that human videos are an incredibly rich prior about how to interact with the world, and we still use them today. But it also pushed me toward simulation, synthetic data, and real robot learning, where the agent can actually act, fail, and correct itself. I now think the right recipe combines the scale of internet data for priors with physically grounded data for real capability.

fable-5.1.text:
That early work was really a child of the internet AI era, and I think it's useful to be honest about both what it got right and what it fundamentally couldn't do.

When I started looking at human–object interactions in videos, the appeal was obvious: the internet had this enormous supply of people doing things with objects. Opening doors, pouring water, picking up cups, screwing on lids. If you believed, as most of us did at the time, that the bottleneck in AI was data and that supervision could be scraped from the world rather than paid for, then video seemed like the richest free signal available. You could learn what a "grasp" looks like, how a hand approaches a handle, what the typical motion trajectory is for a given object category, all without touching a robot.

And some of that worked. We learned good visual representations of hands and objects, we learned priors about contact and affordance, we could predict plausible future poses. That line of research fed into what people now call visual pretraining for manipulation, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But what the work taught me, almost by frustration, was where internet AI stops. A video shows you the outcome of an interaction, never the causes. You see the hand close on the cup, but you don't see the forces, you don't see the small corrections the person made when the cup was heavier than expected, you don't see the dozens of micro-decisions that made the action succeed. The camera observes a third-person projection of a closed-loop process. So you end up learning a very good model of what interactions look like, and a very poor model of how to produce one.

That's the gap between internet AI and what I'd call embodied AI. Internet data is passive, observational, and largely outcome-only. Embodiment requires intervention: you act, the world pushes back, and you update. No amount of YouTube footage gives you that feedback loop. It gives you the vocabulary of interaction, not the grammar.

So looking back, I'd describe that early research as the moment I realized that vision could get us to the doorstep of manipulation but not through the door. It shaped how I think about the problem now: use internet-scale video for what it's genuinely good at, which is semantic and geometric priors, and then be very deliberate about where real physical interaction, simulation, or robot data has to take over. The two aren't in competition. The mistake would be assuming the first can substitute for the second.

astra-6.text:
I see that early work as a bridge between learning from internet data and understanding the physical world. Videos contain a lot of information about how people interact with objects: how they grasp something, move it, and use it to accomplish a task. The challenge is to recover that interaction, rather than just recognize the person and the object.

That connects naturally to internet AI, because video offers a way to learn from human experience at scale. But observing an action is different from being able to perform it. You can watch someone pick up a cup without knowing the forces involved or how to adjust when it starts slipping. So learning from video can provide a useful foundation, while physical interaction is needed to ground and refine that understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I see that early work as a step toward learning how the physical world works from the information available on the internet. Videos show people grasping objects, moving them, and using them to accomplish tasks. The interesting question is whether AI can learn more than what an action looks like—whether it can learn the relationship between the person, the object, and the resulting change.

That connects naturally to internet AI, but there is also a gap. Watching someone interact with an object does not automatically give a system the ability to perform that interaction. Video provides observations; acting requires understanding things like geometry, contact, and the consequences of your own movements. So I see learning from video as an important source of knowledge, with the challenge being how to turn that knowledge into the ability to act.
